concepts.name: Medium of Exchange: Core Function and Limitations
key_dimensions: How money eliminates the 'double coincidence of wants' problem inherent in barter
Conditions under which money fails as medium of exchange (hyperinflation, loss of trust)
Distinction between legal tender (compulsory acceptance) vs. money as medium of exchange
Crypto-assets and digital tokens as emerging mediums of exchange — UPSC trap on legal tender status

concepts.name: Unit of Account (Measure of Value): Standard of Value Function
key_dimensions: How a common unit of account enables price comparison and economic calculation
Distinction between 'unit of account' and 'store of value' — commonly confused in UPSC MCQs
Role in national income accounting, budgeting, and balance of payments measurement
Inflation's distortion of unit of account function — real vs. nominal value trap

concepts.name: Store of Value: Money vs. Other Assets
key_dimensions: Money as an imperfect store of value due to inflation erosion
Comparison: money vs. gold, real estate, bonds as stores of value
Liquidity preference theory (Keynes) — why people hold money despite it being an inferior store of value
UPSC trap: Store of value is NOT unique to money — shares this function with many assets

concepts.name: Standard of Deferred Payment: Credit and Debt Enablement
key_dimensions: Definition: Money as the unit in which future payments (loans, EMIs, bonds) are denominated
Debate on whether this is a primary or derived function of money
Inflation and deflation effects on debtors vs. creditors — redistributive consequences
UPSC trap: Some economists (e.g., Crowther) classify this as a secondary/derivative function, not primary

concepts.name: Primary vs. Secondary (Derivative) Functions of Money: Classification Debate
key_dimensions: Primary functions: Medium of exchange + Measure of value (universally agreed)
Secondary functions: Store of value + Standard of deferred payment (debated classification)
Contingent/tertiary functions: Distribution of income, maximization of utility, basis of credit
UPSC trap: Different economists (Walker, Keynes, Crowther, Robertson) use different classification frameworks

concepts.name: Contingent (Tertiary) Functions of Money: Credit, Distribution, and Utility
key_dimensions: Basis of credit creation: How money in banks enables credit multiplier effect
Distribution of national income: Money enables factor payments (rent, wages, interest, profit)
Maximization of utility and productivity: Enables rational allocation via price signals
UPSC trap: These are often tested as 'which of the following is NOT a primary function of money'

concepts.name: Liquidity of Money: Spectrum of Liquidity Across Money Forms
key_dimensions: Definition of liquidity and why cash (M0) is the most liquid asset
Liquidity spectrum: Currency > Demand deposits > Time deposits > Near-money
Near-money (Treasury bills, commercial paper) — liquid but NOT money: key UPSC distinction
Keynes's liquidity trap — when liquidity preference renders monetary policy ineffective

concepts.name: Money Supply Aggregates: M0, M1, M2, M3, M4 — RBI Classification
key_dimensions: Definitions: M0 (Reserve Money/High-powered money), M1 (Narrow money), M3 (Broad money/L1)
Components of each: Currency with public, demand deposits, time deposits, post office deposits
M3 as the most commonly referenced policy target — why RBI monitors M3 growth
UPSC trap: M4 includes post office total deposits (including NSC) — distinguishing M3 vs. M4

concepts.name: High-Powered Money (Monetary Base / Reserve Money): Creation and Multiplier
key_dimensions: Components: Currency in circulation + Banker's deposits with RBI + Other deposits with RBI
How RBI creates high-powered money: OMO, CRR changes, government borrowing
Money multiplier formula: M = 1/CRR (simplified) and its real-world limitations
UPSC trap: High-powered money ≠ M1; it is the BASE from which M1, M3 are derived

concepts.name: Barter System vs. Monetary Economy: Inefficiencies and Transition
key_dimensions: Four problems of barter: Double coincidence, lack of divisibility, store of value, deferred payment
How each function of money directly solves a specific barter problem — mapping exercise
Primitive forms of money (commodity money, metallic money) as transitional stages
UPSC trap: Barter still exists in modern economies (countertrade, crypto-barter) — not fully obsolete

concepts.name: Commodity Money vs. Fiat Money vs. Credit Money: Evolution and Trust
key_dimensions: Commodity money (intrinsic value) → Representative money → Fiat money (government decree)
Fiat money's value based purely on government authority and public trust — no intrinsic backing
Credit money: Cheques, bills of exchange — money created by commercial banking system
UPSC trap: Indian Rupee is fiat money, NOT backed by gold since 1971 (end of Bretton Woods)

concepts.name: Legal Tender: Limited vs. Unlimited Legal Tender in India
key_dimensions: Legal tender defined: Money that must be accepted by law in settlement of debt
Unlimited legal tender: All RBI notes (₹2 and above) — must be accepted for any amount
Limited legal tender: Coins — acceptance limited by law (e.g., small coins up to ₹1000 in certain transactions)
UPSC trap: ₹1 coin and note are issued by Government of India, NOT RBI — critical distinction

concepts.name: Neutrality of Money: Classical vs. Keynesian Debate
key_dimensions: Classical/Quantity Theory: Money is neutral — changes in money supply only affect price level, not real output
Keynesian critique: Money is non-neutral in short run — affects output, employment via aggregate demand
Quantity Theory of Money (Fisher's MV = PT) and its assumptions
UPSC trap: Modern consensus — money is non-neutral in short run but neutral in long run

concepts.name: Quantity Theory of Money (Fisher's Equation): MV = PT
key_dimensions: Variables: M (money supply), V (velocity of circulation), P (price level), T (volume of transactions)
Key assumptions: V and T are constant in short run — making P directly proportional to M
Cambridge Cash Balance Approach (Marshall-Pigou): M = kPY — demand-side variation
UPSC trap: Velocity of money is NOT constant — falls during recession (liquidity trap), undermining the theory

concepts.name: Velocity of Money: Concept, Measurement, and Policy Implications
key_dimensions: Definition: Number of times a unit of money changes hands in a given period
Factors affecting velocity: Payment habits, banking development, income levels, inflation expectations
Demonetization 2016 impact: Sharp fall in velocity of money — real-world UPSC case study
UPSC trap: Higher velocity can be inflationary even without increase in money supply

concepts.name: Motives for Holding Money (Liquidity Preference Theory — Keynes)
key_dimensions: Three motives: Transactions motive, Precautionary motive, Speculative motive
Speculative motive: Inverse relationship between interest rate and money demand — key Keynesian insight
Liquidity trap: Interest rates so low that everyone prefers holding cash over bonds — monetary policy becomes ineffective
UPSC trap: Transactions + Precautionary motives are interest-inelastic; Speculative motive is interest-elastic

concepts.name: Digital Money and E-Money: CBDC, UPI, and Functional Equivalence
key_dimensions: Digital Rupee (e₹): RBI's Central Bank Digital Currency — wholesale (e₹-W) vs. retail (e₹-R)
How CBDC performs all four functions of money in digital form — functional equivalence with physical currency
Distinction: CBDC (liability of RBI/central bank) vs. bank deposits (liability of commercial bank)
UPSC trap: UPI/NEFT transfers are NOT money — they are payment mechanisms moving bank money; CBDC IS money

concepts.name: Near-Money and Quasi-Money: Distinction from True Money
key_dimensions: Near-money: Assets easily convertible to money but not directly usable — Treasury bills, FDs, savings bonds
Quasi-money: Broader concept including near-money + instruments like traveler's cheques
Why near-money is excluded from M1 but included in M3/M4 — liquidity gradient logic
UPSC trap: Near-money performs 'store of value' function but NOT 'medium of exchange' — partial money function

concepts.name: Inflation's Impact on Functions of Money: Functional Degradation
key_dimensions: Mild inflation: Medium of exchange and unit of account functions largely intact
High inflation: Store of value function severely eroded — flight to real assets (gold, land)
Hyperinflation (e.g., Zimbabwe, Weimar Germany): All functions collapse — barter re-emerges
UPSC trap: Deflation also damages money functions — deferred payment becomes burdensome for debtors, reducing exchange

concepts.name: Money vs. Currency vs. Legal Tender: Overlapping but Distinct Concepts
key_dimensions: Currency: Coins + paper notes (subset of money); Money: broader (includes deposits, credit)
Legal tender: Legally mandated acceptance — not all money is legal tender (cheques are not)
Cheques, demand drafts: Money (perform exchange function) but NOT legal tender — can be refused
UPSC trap: All legal tender is money, but NOT all money is legal tender — classic UPSC reversal question
